steps.title: The rule
steps.say: Every valve in the heart is passive. It opens only when the pressure behind it is higher than the pressure in front, and it shuts the moment that reverses. Watch the four valves and the pressures beside each chamber, and the whole cycle explains itself.

steps.title: The spark
steps.say: Every beat starts with an electrical wave. The pacemaker cell in the S A node has no stable resting voltage, so it drifts up to threshold and fires on its own. The wave sweeps across the atria, which is the P wave, then waits in the A V node for about a tenth of a second. It then races down the bundle of His and the Purkinje fibres, and the ventricular cells fire together. That is the Q R S, and their long plateau is why the heart cannot be tetanised.

steps.title: Atrial kick
steps.say: Now the atria contract. In the lens we are looking down at the mitral valve from inside the left atrium, the way a surgeon sees it. While left atrial pressure is above left ventricular pressure, the two leaflets part, and the atrium tops up the ventricle with its last fifth of filling. The ventricle reaches its end-diastolic volume, about 125 millilitres here.

steps.title: Isovolumetric contraction
steps.say: The ventricles now contract. Calcium floods out of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, myosin heads grab actin and pull, and tension rises. As soon as ventricular pressure passes the atrium, the mitral valve shuts, which is the first heart sound. But pressure is still below the aorta's 80, so the aortic valve stays shut too. With both valves closed, the sarcomere cannot shorten: tension climbs at a fixed length and a fixed volume.

steps.title: Ejection
steps.say: When left ventricular pressure passes about 80 millimetres of mercury, the aortic valve is forced open. In the lens we are looking straight down the aorta, and the three cusps fold back into a triangle as blood jets towards us. Pressure in the ventricle and aorta rises together to about 120. The right ventricle ejects the same volume into the lungs at only about 20.

steps.title: Stroke volume
steps.say: Plot ventricular pressure against volume, and one beat draws one loop. The bottom edge is filling, the right edge is isovolumetric contraction, the top is ejection and the left edge is relaxation. Each corner is a valve opening or closing. The loop's width is the stroke volume: about 125 minus 55, which is 70 millilitres, an ejection fraction of about 55 percent.

steps.title: Heart sounds
steps.say: Now the ventricle relaxes. Its pressure falls below the aorta, a brief backflow snaps the aortic valve shut, and that is the second heart sound and the dicrotic notch. You hear valves closing, never opening. The second sound is best heard at the second intercostal spaces beside the sternum, and the first at the apex, in the fifth space in the mid-clavicular line.

steps.title: Rapid filling
steps.say: When ventricular pressure falls below the atrium, the mitral and tricuspid valves open, and blood that pooled in the atria rushes in. In this slice across the ventricles, watch the thick left ventricular wall thin out again as its cavity refills, and the thin right ventricle wrapped around it. Most filling happens now, passively, before the atria ever contract.

steps.title: Diastasis
steps.say: Atrial and ventricular pressures have nearly equalised, so filling slows to a trickle, fed straight through from the veins. Then the next P wave fires, and the cycle repeats about 75 times a minute, each beat taking 0.8 seconds.
